docs.title: About me
docs.text:
Design with your heart, make with your mind, and share with those who taught you.

I'm Ben Levi, the developer behind the BLV open-source 3D printers. I learned most of what I know about 3D printing from the early community forums, where every comment and thread was valuable and laid the foundations for what we all use today.

Each BLV project took more than 300 hours of design, testing and documentation. I did it alongside a day job that has nothing to do with 3D printing, a wife and two young children. It wasn't easy, but this work became a kind of therapy for me and brought back a passion I thought I had lost.

Sharing is the reason the projects exist. When the FDM patent expired, open sharing of knowledge is what turned 3D printing into what it is now. If everyone had kept their findings to themselves, none of it would exist. The BLV projects are my way of giving back, so they are free for non-commercial use, with all the files, guides and CAD sources included.

The projects are no longer updated, and this site keeps them available as an archive.

Sincerely yours,Ben Levi

If you'd like to support my work, a small donation is greatly appreciated.

docs.title: BLV Ender 3 Pro
docs.text:
Upgrade mod

The BLV Ender 3 Pro is an upgrade project for the popular Ender 3 Pro 3D printer. It replaces the printed and wheel-based parts with all-aluminum parts, MGN12 linear rails and a BMG dual drive extruder, for better accuracy, efficiency and print quality.

Download all files Thingiverse Remixes Facebook group

BLV Ender 3 Pro

Kits are no longer sold

The ready-made BLV Ender 3 Pro aluminum kits are no longer available. The drawings and files are still here, so the parts can be made by a CNC service for personal use.

docs.title: Why build it
docs.text:
• Fast, reliable, accurate. Low and mid range printers usually move on linear bearings or Delrin wheels because they are cheap, and the price is accuracy and reliability. MGN linear rails are stiffer, more precise and smoother, so prints are faster without losing quality. That is why high-end printers use them. If you are tired of worn POM wheels that need constant tightening, this upgrade is for you.
  • Rigid parts. This project takes a different path from the earlier ones. Printed parts flex a little, so CNC machined aluminum parts replace them. To test the difference I logged a dial indicator to a database on my PC. After more than 2000 measuring loops of uniformity and deviation, the aluminum parts gave clearly better results than printed parts.
  • Accessible. CNC parts are usually expensive. To keep the cost down, the design was offered free for commercial use with my permission. Design time (more than 200 hours here) is a large part of the price of such parts, so manufacturers could sell the kit for less. While it was on sale, 4 aluminum parts typically sold for $30 or more on AliExpress, and this kit had 16 pieces for $59, including belts, screws and shipping. Other aluminum and rail kits cost $300 or more.
  • Open source. Why give the work away? I learned everything I know about 3D printing from this community, and the BLV projects are my way of giving back. The same idea is behind the BLV mgn Cube and the BLV Anet mod. When the FDM patent expired, open sharing of knowledge is what built everything we have now. Imagine if everyone had kept their findings to themselves.

The upgrade was tested for over 700 hours of printing before release.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Prepare. Read the project description, watch the 3D animation videos and make sure you understand the structure.
  2. Get the parts. Order everything in the BOM, plus spare T-nuts and screws, and prepare the tools.
  3. Build. A precise frame is the basis of good prints, and several YouTube videos show how to align the Ender 3 Pro frame. Use the printed jigs when installing the MGN rails. They make the assembly much easier. Take your time fixing the rails to the extrusions. This short video by 3D Distributed shows an easy way to align parallel rails.
  4. Install the electronics. For the SKR Mini E3 V1.2 board there is a good YouTube installation guide. The Duet WiFi 1.04 board is also an option.
  5. Software, tests and calibration. This step needs some experience, or one of the many YouTube guides on calibrating the Ender 3 Pro. I recommend a fresh Marlin build instead of the original firmware. Don't skip: wiring and endstop check, firmware update, extruder and feed rate calibration, hotend and bed PID, and the probe Z offset.
  6. Print and maintain. Grease the rails with white lithium grease or light sewing machine oil. Keep the rails clean and the belts tight. Clean the PEI plate with alcohol after every print, and lightly scuff new sheets with brass wool.
  7. Share your build. Post an "I made one" photo. Knowing the project helped you makes all the hours worth it.
  8. Remix and share. The source files are included so you can improve the design. Please share your remixes with the community.
  9. Commercial use. Read the legal license first.

Requirements

An Ender 3 Pro (the Pro version only, its 4040 Y extrusion is part of the design), the aluminum upgrade parts from the BOM, basic technical skills and a few free evenings.

docs.title: Hotend
docs.text:
A better hotend is a recommended upgrade. First decide between Bowden and direct drive.

BowdenDirect drive
  • The original Creality hotend, or a cheap clone
  • High quality hotend by Mellow
  • Excellent quality hotend by Trianglelab
  • Dragon V2 hotend, excellent results

Trianglelab DDE direct drive, 24V full set, a great system.

Its X carriage is very similar to the original Ender carriage. To install the DDE, drill two small holes for M3×6 mm screws in the carriage. It takes about 2 minutes (how).

With the Trianglelab DDE, use the two screws for alignment only, then remove them.

docs.title: Z axis
docs.text:
Choose a Z setup:

  1. Single Z stepper. It worked well for me for a while, but dual Z adds rigidity and greatly improves the Z axis.
  2. Dual Z with one stepper. A dual Z set with one stepper, 2 threaded rods and a belt. This BMG bracket recovers some of the lost Z height. Some height is still lost because the extruder touches the left top plate, but this became my favorite setup. Replace the Phillips screws that come with the set with hex socket head screws.
  3. Dual Z with two steppers. The recommended set for dual Z with a second Z motor. Align the Z axis so both sides match.

Note

Dual Z setups reduce the Z height, since the BMG can touch the top plates.

The original Creality belt is too flexible and reduces print quality. Use a fiberglass-reinforced GT2 6 mm belt instead. The X axis belt is clamped at a length of 785 mm, measured between the clamps and not including the brass clamps. When replacing a belt, both ends can be locked with a zip tie.

Build volume. To keep the original build volume, change Y_MIN_POS in Marlin's Configuration.h. My value was -9.15. Adjust it to your setup. The picture shows where to find it.

docs.title: Upgrades and tips
docs.text:
Smart filament sensorPEI surfaceLED installationBed carriage springsTrianglelab DDE

Why pay $15 for the SKR smart filament sensor when a wire and an endstop switch cost $1.50? This video explains the difference.

A switch sensor only detects whether filament is present. If the spool jams or the filament gets stuck, nothing happens and the printer keeps printing air. The smart sensor tracks filament movement with a rotary encoder and pauses the print when the filament stops moving. It is well worth it, especially for long prints of 12 hours or more.

After a long time with the Energetic PEI spring steel sheet, I tested the Trianglelab double-coated PEI sheet. It arrived well packed, with alcohol wipes and a printed manual. On the first try the corners lifted. The last tip in the manual solved it: scuff the PEI well with brass wool, and prints stick very well. Unlike the Energetic sheet, prints also release easily once the sheet cools down.

Use a 5V, 60 LEDs/m, non-waterproof strip that can be cut after every LED. The non-waterproof type slides into the V-slot channel more easily.

  1. Cut a 15-LED strip, solder a long 4-wire cable to it, and slide it into the top V-slot channel.
  2. Cut a 3-LED strip, solder a cable to it, and secure it with 2 zip ties to the back of the transparent BMG extruder.
  3. Connect both strips together and check the connection.
  4. Then either:
    • connect them to a simple RGB LED controller and use the IR remote, or
    • connect them to the SKR Mini E3 LED pins and configure them in the firmware.

Replace the original bed springs with the stronger yellow Creality CR-10 springs for a much more stable bed.

To install the Trianglelab DDE system:

  1. Print Carriage template.stl.
  2. Place the drilling template on the rear of the DDE system.
  3. Drill two holes as shown, with a 6 mm drill bit, 4 mm deep.
  4. Remove the template.
  5. Install the DDE on the X carriage.

docs.title: Rail tips
docs.text:
I started with affordable MGN12H rails from AliExpress at about $18 each. After buying from four different sellers, I found the best value at the CNA Mechanical Parts Store. Their carriages slide smoothly straight out of the box, with no cleaning needed. For higher quality at a reasonable price, the HIWIN rail set is excellent.

Sellers to avoid

Avoid RDC Official Store and linkcnc Store on AliExpress. linkcnc sent me a used, damaged rail that was shorter than ordered and stayed stuck even after cleaning. RDC started shipping carriages that don't match the MGN standard.

Cleaning and lubrication. New rails usually feel rough because they are coated with a protective oil at the factory. Clean it off (several YouTube videos show how to clean the carriage with WD-40), then lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or a PTFE silicone grease. These are miniature rails, so avoid thick grease. The goal is a smooth carriage without free play.

The video below shows the cleaning process well. Work over a container so you don't lose any steel balls. After reassembly there is room for one more ball, which is normal.

Tuning up cheap Chinese linear bearings

Mounting the rails takes patience. They must be perfectly straight and aligned, and rushing this step causes problems later.

Don't rely on the gravity test

Tilting a rail and watching the carriage slide down says nothing about its quality. A rail with too much free play passes easily and then fails every print quality test. The tolerance grade of the rail sets the friction of the carriage.

docs.title: BLV Ender 3 Pro upgrade project
docs.text:
Hi friends, after a lot of hard work, the new open-source project is alive. This upgrade will boost your Ender 3 Pro's performance. Your Ender 3 Pro will be quieter, more rigid and more accurate, and it will produce high-quality prints. No more worn-out POM wheels, no more eccentric nut adjustments, no more loose axes or free play. Just pure, accurate motion on all axes using linear rails!

Instead of using flexible 3D printed parts as adapters, I designed 16 parts that are fully CNC machined from aluminum for a structure that is as rigid as possible.

As always, the project is open source ☺️ and I'm trying my best to make it affordable and accessible to all. By giving all my hard work (200+ hours) to the manufacturer for free (it's a non-profit project) and saving them the development cost, the manufacturers are willing to produce the kit cheaply.

docs.title: BLV mgn Cube
docs.text:
Open-source 3D printer

The BLV mgn Cube is an open front CoreXY 3D printer that runs on MGN linear rails. It was designed for accuracy, efficiency and print quality, with one simple goal: to let anyone build a good and reliable 3D printer.

1.78Mdownloads6.3Mviews

Start building Bill of materials Download the files

BLV mgn Cube at 9000 mm/s² acceleration and 500 mm/s

docs.title: Why build it
docs.text:
• Fast, reliable, accurate. Most low and mid range printers ride on linear bearings or Delrin wheels because they are cheap, and they give up accuracy and reliability for it. MGN linear rails are stiffer, more precise and much smoother, so the Cube prints fast without losing quality.
  • Rigid open structure. The open front is as rigid as a closed cube and still gives easy access to the bed. The design came out of many hours of simulation and physical stress tests. A front belt tensioner keeps maintenance simple.
  • Accessible. There are no rare or expensive machined parts. Everything is printed or bought online or locally, and you can use your own electronics if you know how to adapt the firmware.
  • Open source. The original STEP files are included. Remix and improve them, and please share your work, mark the parts as remixed and link back to the project.
  • Ready to print. Tuned firmware settings and slicer profiles are included. Upload the configuration, load the profile and print.
  • Modular. Height and bed size can grow with longer extrusions and rails. A size calculator helps you plan a custom build.
  • Honest about the effort. Installing and aligning the rails takes about 70% of the build time. 3D animations, PDF guides, sketches and measurements make it manageable.
  • Balanced budget. A top 32-bit board, good motors and reliable sensors, without overspending. The 5" PanelDue screen is optional. A phone or tablet works just as well and saves about $80.

docs.title: Hotend
docs.text:
The original BLV mgn Cube had official Bowden and direct drive options. The Metal Kit adds a Bowden option with twin blowers and direct drive setups for the BIQU H2 and the Trianglelab Matrix.

The community also created a large variety of hotends for every version, including a tool changer. Browse the community remixes to find the hotend that fits your needs. The drawings below cover several BLV hotend versions and help with the assembly and the exact auto-leveling coordinates.

Many of the best hotend solutions came from the community, including a BLV Cube tool changer and EVA 2.3.0 support. They are collected on the community remixes page.

docs.title: Optional components
docs.text:
Taller ZAir scrubbersHeated bedCOB LED lighting

For a printer taller than standard, add a 496 mm reinforcing extrusion at the top, just below the front tensioners, as in the picture. It keeps the frame stable at any height.

The project includes a small and a large air scrubber. Printing releases fine particles into the air, and the scrubbers filter them.

Mount the fan so it pushes the air into the filter. The air should pass through the activated carbon first and then through the HEPA filter. Check the filters monthly and replace them when needed.

The best bed is an aluminum MIC6 plate with an AC silicone heater, but it has two drawbacks:

  1. Cost. Both the MIC6 plate and the silicone heater are relatively expensive.
  2. Risk of electric shock if it is not installed correctly.

A 24V bed heats more slowly than an AC bed but is safe to use. The FYSETC parts set came with a magnetic aluminum bed and a BuildTak-like glass surface, which is flat and easy to handle. The original Blurolls set came with a PCB bed, which I recommend less because it tends to warp at high temperatures.

These pictures show the FYSETC bed (see my FYSETC unboxing). The bed parts are also listed in the BOM. Install the magnetic surface layers in exactly the order shown.

After a long time with a regular LED strip, I wanted lighting that is hidden, needs no printed parts and shines evenly instead of in spots. The answer was a COB LED strip.

A COB strip has much smaller diodes, about 360 per meter instead of 60, so the light is even. A silicone layer over the diodes works as a diffuser. The strip is also narrow. The 8 mm version slides straight into the extrusion channel. It can be cut every 50 mm and the brightness can be controlled.

The first two strips I ordered from different AliExpress stores were disappointing. Then I found a reliable store with good COB strips. My choice was 6000K cool white, 24V, 360 LEDs per meter, 2 meters.

  1. Cut the strip at the marks (every 50 mm) with scissors.
  2. Solder two 26AWG wires, or use this quick connector (choose "For 8 mm PCB") if you prefer not to solder.
  3. Slide the strip into the upper extrusion channels.
  4. Connect the wires in one of two ways:
    • Directly to a 24V PSU
    • To a Duet fan output, which lets you set the brightness with a slider in the Duet control panel

I use the Duet 3 6HC board from FYSETC, so I defined the lights as a fan output with this line in config.g and connected the strip to the OUT9 port:

M950 F2 C"out9" Q500 M106 P2 S0.2 H-1 C"Lights"

The result is efficient, good-looking light with adjustable brightness from the panel.

docs.title: Linear rail tips
docs.text:
I started with affordable MGN12H rails from AliExpress at about $18 each. After buying from four different sellers, I found the best value at the CNA Mechanical Parts Store. Their carriages slide smoothly straight out of the box, with no cleaning needed. For higher quality at a reasonable price, the HIWIN rail set is excellent.

Sellers to avoid

Avoid RDC Official Store and linkcnc Store on AliExpress. linkcnc sent me a used, damaged rail that was shorter than ordered and stayed stuck even after cleaning. RDC started shipping carriages that don't match the MGN standard.

Cleaning and lubrication. New rails usually feel rough because they are coated with a protective oil at the factory. Clean it off (several YouTube videos show how to clean the carriage with WD-40), then lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or a PTFE silicone grease. These are miniature rails, so avoid thick grease. The goal is a smooth carriage without free play.

The video below shows the cleaning process well. Work over a container so you don't lose any steel balls. After reassembly there is room for one more ball, which is normal.

Tuning up cheap Chinese linear bearings

Mounting the rails takes patience. They must be perfectly straight and aligned, and rushing this step causes problems later.

Don't rely on the gravity test

Tilting a rail and watching the carriage slide down says nothing about its quality. A rail with too much free play passes easily and then fails every print quality test. The tolerance grade of the rail sets the friction of the carriage.

docs.title: Calibrations
docs.text: Before calibrating, make sure the Duet board runs the right firmware. The project was released on RepRap 2.x and later moved to the Duet 3 board with RepRap 3.x. Community member David Husolo published well-tuned BLV Cube configuration files on GitHub for both the Duet 2 WiFi and the Duet 3 running RepRap 3.x.

docs.title: 1. Update the Duet firmware
docs.text:
Duet boards are very well documented, with step-by-step guides for almost every task. Update to the latest RepRap firmware 3.x before calibrating. The Duet 2 WiFi and the Duet 3 use the same update guide.

Download the firmware Update guide

docs.title: 2. Copy the config files
docs.text:
Copy the BLV configuration files to the SD card. If the card is new or empty, prepare it first as described in the Duet documentation.

Your setup Config files RepRap 3.x (recommended) David Husolo's GitHub, "firmware" folder. Thank you David! FYSETC parts set FYSETC firmware for the BLV mgn Cube RepRap 2.x The SD card ZIP in the project files. One ZIP is a basic Duet 3 configuration, the other is for RepRap 2.x only.

docs.title: 3. Connect to the web interface
docs.text:
The Duet has a built-in web interface with full control of the printer, from any phone, tablet or computer on your network. The Duet documentation explains the network setup, and the Duet Web Control manual covers the interface itself.

Avoid damaging the hardware

  • Never disconnect cables from a powered Duet, except the USB cable.
  • Check all wires for shorts, especially fan, motor and heater wires.
  • Don't feed the board more than 24 volts.
  • Ground the frame and the bed carriage, and the motors if possible.
  • Don't scratch, short or damage the electronics while installing them.
  • Don't remove the memory card while the printer is running.
  • Take your time crimping connectors and check the wires with a multimeter.
  • Triple check the polarity and position of every connection.
  • With the steppers connected, don't move an axis quickly by hand.

docs.title: 4. Configure your printer
docs.text:
The provided configuration covers almost everything. You may still want to center the bed, set motor directions, add macro buttons or define temperature presets per filament. The Duet guides cover all of this.

Start with the RepRap 3 overview, which is essential reading. Then complete these before moving on:

  • Center your bed
  • Test your endstop switches
  • Set up a different Z probe, only for other probe types
  • Set up a PT100 sensor, only with a PT100

docs.title: Stepper motors
docs.text:
With the FYSETC parts set you can skip this, since its labeled cables match the FYSETC configuration. With steppers from the BOM or the Blurolls set, the motors will probably turn the wrong way at first. Set them up like this:

  1. Identify the coil pairs. A stepper has 4 wires, 2 per coil. This short guide and this video show how to find them.
  2. Connect the steppers using the original Duet stepper wiring, shown in the bottom right corner of wiring diagram v3.2 under "Duet original steppers wiring".
  3. Test and configure them with the Duet documentation. The video shows the expected movement for each test command.
  4. Check the directions. In the third video I press the jog buttons. Your printer should move the same way.
Identify the leads of a 4-wire stepper with a multimeterSteppers testAxis movement

More guides:

  • Tuning stepper motor drivers for the Duet's TMC2660 drivers
  • Mesh bed compensation to change the mesh settings
  • Multiple independent Z motors for true auto leveling
  • Filament sensor

docs.title: 5. Calibrate
docs.text:
These calibrations are mandatory. Follow the pictures exactly and work accurately, since they have a large effect on print quality: the Z probe height first, then PID tuning for the hotend and the bed.

Hotend PID. The pictures show the classic hotend PID tuning. Newer RepRap 3.x releases add an algorithm that detects fan speed changes and adjusts the heater in advance. To use it:

  • Run the latest 3.x release.
  • Define all your tools (T0) correctly.
  • Define your fans according to the RRF instructions.
  • Turn off the part cooling fan and run M303 T0 S200, with 200 replaced by your usual printing temperature. The algorithm turns the fan on by itself during tuning.

In short, replace M303 H1 S190 with M303 T0 S190.

docs.text:
Read each guide before enabling the feature.

  • Stall detection and sensorless homing
  • Pressure advance to compensate for filament and extruder elasticity
  • Resume a print after a power failure

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
This page is the road map of the build. Read it once before ordering anything, then follow the guide pages in order: BOM, Download & Print, Assembly, Wiring and Calibrations.

Before you begin

This is not a kit you assemble in an evening. Expect some 3D printing experience, basic electronics skills, a few weekends of work and a mid-range budget. In return you get a printer you understand down to the last screw.

docs.title: The build, step by step
docs.text:
1. Prepare. Read the project description and the linked material, watch the 3D animations and explore the printer in the 3D viewer. Make sure you understand the structure before you start.
  2. Get the parts. Waiting for parts is the most frustrating stage. Check that you have everything in the BOM, plus spare T-nuts and screws. If you use your own electronics, make sure you know how to configure the firmware for your board.
  3. Build. Prepare the tools and use a good corner alignment tool. A precise frame is the basis of good prints. The printed jigs make the assembly much easier. Tap the holes in the extrusion ends and check whether they take M5 or M6 screws, since this depends on the extrusion maker. Take your time with the rails. This short video by 3D Distributed shows an easy way to align parallel rails. Reward yourself when the rails are in, you deserve it.
  4. Install the electronics. Check every connection against the wiring diagram, avoid shortcuts and use the right tools and parts. Connect the power cable last.
  5. Test and calibrate. Update the Duet board to the latest firmware, copy the provided configuration to the micro SD card, insert it and power up. The Mini IR sensor should blink 4 times at power-up. Check the endstops before you move any axis. When you home the printer it should move left and then to the rear. If it doesn't, check the motor wiring and the configuration. Calibrate the Z height and check the temperature readings. Run a PID calibration for both the bed and the hotend. This step is essential. Without it, prints will fail. When everything looks right, load filament and print a calibration cube. Details are on the Calibrations page.
  6. Print and maintain. Grease the rails with a synthetic PTFE grease or sewing machine oil. Keep the rails clean and the belts tight. Clean the PEI plate with alcohol after every print. If you built the air scrubber, replace the HEPA filter when needed.
  7. Share your build. I would really appreciate an "I made one" photo. Knowing the project helped you build your own printer makes all the hours worth it.
  8. Remix and share. There are many ways to make this printer better, which is why the source files are included. Improve it and share your remixes with the community.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Wiring is a critical step, so double check every wire. It usually takes about 3 hours. With the FYSETC parts set it takes about an hour, since that set came with an optimized diagram, ready-made labeled cables with plugs, stepper wires in the correct order and a plug-and-play PCB for the Neopixel rings. Follow the diagram that matches your setup.

Before you start

  • Wire the printer with the AC plug disconnected.
  • Crimp every cable that goes into the power supply.
  • Don't mix negative and positive wires.
  • Double check every wire.

Click a diagram to open it full size. Zoom in to read the pin labels.

Duet 2 WiFiDuet 3 6HCFYSETC parts set

Three diagrams: the main wiring (v3.2), 12V fans on a 24V system (wire 12V fans this way to protect the board and the fans), and the Neopixel rings on the front panel that show the printer status with animations. Arduino code for the rings: latest code by Claus Noack (confirmed working) or the first alpha by Mimasx.

Wiring diagram for the Duet 3 6HC board. Fans, heaters and the Neopixel rings follow the same logic as the Duet 2 diagrams.

Four diagrams for the FYSETC parts set: the optimized general wiring, the BLTouch auto-leveling sensor, the power button with relay module, and the FYSETC BLV Neopixel module. The Neopixel module is a 5-minute install: the cables are ready, the rings come with soldered pins, and the 2-pin and 3-pin plugs only fit one way.

docs.title: BIQU H2O and Haldis K1-XL hotend
docs.text: I want to share my first impressions, or shall I say unboxing, of a few hotend-extruder setups I'm testing. I'm sure it's going to be interesting. As you know, I try to be very thorough. Reaching full conclusions about an extruder or any particular component takes me about two full months of non-stop printing. Until then, I only allow myself to write about initial impressions.

docs.title: BIQU H2O - new extruder
docs.text:
I can sum up everything I write below about the BIQU H2O in one word: beautiful.

The new BIQU H2O arrived while I was busy working on the BLV Metal Kit II, so it had to wait. If I had only known what I was missing. I have not been this impressed with an extruder in a long time.

You're probably asking: why do I even need a water-cooled extruder?

I am not a fan of ABS printing, and most of the time I print PLA, PETG, flex and so on. But I have small children, and a closed enclosure keeps odors and particles away from them. Inside the enclosure the temperatures are much higher than without it, which can make it difficult to print common filaments. Water cooling is part of the solution.

Now let's get back to the new H2O extruder. I'm sure you have already seen my review of the original H2 extruder. A lot of improvements went into the new extruder, and it looks like someone at BIQU did their homework. It is equipped with a high-temperature resistant motor (180°C) and stainless steel gears (according to the spec). I just wish they were hardened stainless steel. They added a MAX31865 module to support the included PT-100 sensor, which is a much more accurate temperature sensor at high temperatures. One more important thing: the bi-metal heatbreak is made of copper and titanium, not aluminum. As you know, aluminum can damage your water cooling system over time.

Another thing I really like is the sleek look. Everything is symmetrical, with clean lines. Very elegant! The RGB LEDs illuminating the water chamber are lovely. I almost forgot to mention that the new H2O is very small. It is even 11.6 mm smaller than the previous H2, and it weighs only 224 g. Check the photos below and notice the window that has been added for the hub wheel.

Here's the full list of accessories that came in the package:

  • BIQU yellow ducky - without it, I would probably have opened a dispute 🤣
  • Full assembly manual, including firmware settings
  • BIQU H2O, fully assembled
  • Copper-nickel plated heating block (assembled)
  • Hardened steel 0.4 mm nozzle (assembled)
  • Copper and titanium bi-metal heatbreak (assembled)
  • Fittings / connectors for ID4/OD6 tubes
  • KJH 04-M6 pneumatic connector for the PTFE tube
  • High-quality PT-100 temperature sensor
  • MAX31865 StepStick module (for the PT-100)
  • JST connector and terminals
  • Orange silicone sock
  • 24V 70W heater cartridge
  • Long motor cable
  • RGB LED cable
  • Screws
  • All the needed tools

docs.title: So does it print well?
docs.text: So far I'm getting fantastic results and I haven't had any problems. But I have to postpone my full conclusions until I reach at least 300 hours of printing. I used the adapter from the previous BIQU H2 and it works great. For now, I am absolutely in love with this extruder. BIQU, you got me!

docs.title: BIQU water cooling system
docs.text:
Then I realized I had thrown away all the water cooling systems from my old computers. Luckily, BIQU offered a new 24V water cooling system that is meant to suit the new BIQU H2O. Even though I ordered it after the extruder, the water cooling system arrived first.

The water cooling system was packed nicely, with all the needed accessories and even more. It includes all the tools you need, even a liquid funnel. The most important part is the pump. In this case it's the 12V SysCooling P67D pump, which is very reliable: 500 L/h max flow, ceramic bearings with a 50k-hour lifetime, a 25-27 dB sound level and G1/4 thread connectors. BIQU included three types of flexible tubes, brackets, double-sided stickers, tube diameter reducers (for other types of extruders), tools, connectors, screws and a power adapter.

Overall it looks good, but there is definitely room for improvement:

  • Buck converter - the pump is 12V, so they used an LM2596 buck converter to convert 24V to 12V. The LM2596 is a very cheap converter, and in my experience it tends to fail after prolonged use. On the other hand, it's very common, easy to find and costs only $3.
  • Spring clamps - my friend David Husolo drew my attention to the fact that the kit uses clamps that are notorious for leaking. So I used a spare fitting from my PC water cooling system instead.
  • Coolant - no coolant was provided with the system. If you decide to buy it, make sure to get a proper coolant.

Please don't get me wrong, I really like this water cooling system. I once bought a water cooling system from another manufacturer, and a month later the pump stopped working. Of course, they refused to replace it. With the BIQU system I feel more confident, since I have had good experience with SysCooling pumps and I know BIQU has good customer service.

docs.title: Final conclusion?
docs.text: There is no way I am writing a final conclusion now. That will come only after testing the system for a long time, at least two months. I want to make sure there are no leaks, that the pump won't fail over time and that it really meets my requirements. Meanwhile, I can tell you that it works great, it is relatively quiet and the cooling is very effective.

docs.title: Haldis K1-XL new hotend with a unibody nozzle
docs.text:
I got one of the first early-bird units of the new Haldis K1-XL hotend for testing.

Haldis is a relatively new manufacturer in the 3D printer market, but despite being new, their production quality stands out. Unlike a few other stores, they produce everything in-house. This gives them many advantages, including the ability to develop products themselves in a short time. The new Haldis K1-XL hotend is a good example of that. It has a unique unibody nozzle with an obvious advantage: the nozzle can be replaced quickly. How quickly, you ask? Just hit the play button below.

The K1-XL is the same size as a regular V6, but it has a unique structure. At first glance it looks like some sort of Dragon and Mosquito combination, but the truth is that it's very different. The K1-XL has a bi-metal unibody nozzle, which means the whole nozzle and filament path, including the heatsink, can be replaced in a matter of seconds. Very convenient: no need to disassemble parts to clear a blockage, and no more fear of tightening the nozzle too hard or breaking the heatbreak. I love this approach. I was also surprised to find a very small, new type of temperature sensor, which is very refreshing. You can see it in the first picture below.

As for the nozzle itself, it's a copper-nickel plated nozzle with an integrated heatsink on its upper part. At the bottom there is a thread, and the whole nozzle assembly simply screws into the thick heated cylinder. Note that the heated element is thick, and my doubts about heat dissipation turned out to be justified: the red heatsink does not seem to be sufficient. I think it will struggle with high temperatures. In the end, I had to use a Gdstime 4020 dual ball bearing fan to get optimal results.

docs.title: So what came in the package?
docs.text:
Unlike other manufacturers, there is no fancy packaging here. Everything came packed in bubble wrap and plastic bags. That could be because this is the first batch of the Haldis K1-XL.

  • Main frame with an integrated thermistor (thermistor type not specified)
  • Ceramic heating element (no connectors?)
  • 2 x bi-metal unibody 0.4 mm copper nickel-plated nozzles
  • Orange silicone sock
  • PTFE lockers/clips

Unfortunately, for this price I would expect fancier packaging, some tools like a socket screwdriver, a detailed manual, connectors and the right cables. The listing is also missing a lot of information about the heating element, the type of thermistor and the materials.

An important note about something that bothers me: lack of information. I recommend that every manufacturer selling 3D printer parts give full details on the material of each component, the sensor type, the heater type, the maximum temperature range, optimal slicer and firmware settings and so on. It helps customers decide whether to buy the product and how to use it. The less data you provide, the more concerns and failures your customers will have when using your products.

Anyway, let's continue.

Besides the insufficient heat dissipation, I noticed that the ceramic heater opening is too wide. Even after heating the block up to 260°C, when the metal had expanded, it was still too loose. This matters a lot, because there is no efficient heat transfer between the heating element and the heating block. The manufacturer suggested using thermal paste to fill the gap between them. I tried that, and the temperature jumps on the graph got smaller, but in my opinion it was still not enough.

Overall, I think the K1-XL idea is beautiful and very refreshing. The production quality is excellent. However, it needs rigorous testing of how everything works together, and a beta testing group, before it is released to customers. If I could advise the manufacturer, I would change a few things:

  • Fix the gap between the ceramic heater and the metal (like the Trianglelab CHC heater)
  • Provide more details: a spec list, measurements and so on
  • Add tools and connectors
  • Make nice packaging that suits the price

Here is a nice photo of the Trianglelab Rapido, the Haldis K1-XL, the Orbiter V2 and the BIQU H2O. I know, the BIQU is so small, and yet it's both an extruder and a hotend.

docs.title: Final conclusion?
docs.text: Unfortunately, I had to take it off. I get unstable temperatures because of the ceramic heater issue, which can hurt print quality. I really hope this gets resolved, because I like the idea of a unibody nozzle.

docs.title: BIQU Hermit Crab - tool changer?
docs.text:
Samuel Gonzalez from the BLV Facebook group shared his plan to adapt the BIQU Hermit Crab tool changer to the BLV Cube 3D printer.

Later he posted an awesome video of the BIQU Hermit Crab tool changer on his BLV Cube printer:

Inspired by him, I decided to order a BIQU Hermit Crab for testing. So far I have only opened the box and done some dry testing, without mounting it on the printer. Many modifications are needed to fit it to the printer. I was very impressed with the reliability of the locking mechanism, but I have two main concerns that keep me from exploring this option further:

  1. The weight - both the back plate and the front plate are made of aluminum, and they weigh quite a lot. I have a suggestion for BIQU that might make it much lighter: a lot of weight could be removed from both plates by using a thick PCB plate instead of aluminum, while keeping the central locking mechanism in aluminum. The bonus is that you would have even more space for electronic components.
  2. Offset - with the Hermit Crab, the hotend must move 30 mm forward, and that's a lot.

As for the product itself, BIQU continues to deliver very high-quality products, great packaging and a detailed manual. Even a 10-year-old could put it together, with dad helping with the settings, which are also included in the manual.

I hope you enjoyed reading. I promise to share my findings as I search for the perfect setup for the new BLV Cube update.

Sincerely,

Ben Levi

So I opened a new discussion in the BLV Facebook group and asked for your help. I want to thank each and every one of you who took the time to write, ask and share. Your requests are very important to me, as they reflect what community members really need from a printer. So thank you.

I can tell you that it will take quite some time to finish designing the new kit. It is not a matter of a month or two, but a little more. Meanwhile, I can point out that a number of things you requested have been confirmed and will be part of the new Metal Kit II.

Among other things, the planned Metal Kit II will include:

  • High-accuracy shoulder bolts
  • Lighter X-carriage parts
  • Triple Z axes (I'm checking a new mechanism)
  • A rear tensioner that is more suitable for a full enclosure
  • An accelerometer mount (thank you, David)
  • Even easier installation

I also want to make the front plate of the X carriage completely flat, so it will be easier to mount extruders like the NF-Sunrise and the BIQU H2/H2O. For that, I moved the belt lockers to the rear of the plate. Don't worry, I will add many threaded holes to the X panels to make them lighter and suitable for many types of hotends and extruders. I'm so excited! 🤩

docs.title: BLV Carbon X-axis new stock
docs.text:
You left me speechless.

Within a few hours, all of Mellow's BLV carbon X-axis stock was gone. Unfortunately, he managed to produce only 43 pieces right before the Chinese holiday. He already let me know that once they are back from the holiday, they will start making new stock. A few lucky community members have already received the carbon tube and uploaded videos, and I was very impressed. I got feedback on the first 30 pieces from the beta test, and it's really good.

I came across a number of questions about the carbon tubes that I want to answer:

  1. The carbon tube's outer dimension is not exactly 20 mm. What should I do? You shouldn't worry about it. A deviation of 0.3-1 mm in the outer dimensions of a square tube is very common, and it has no effect on the printer's performance or accuracy. Don't forget that the X carriage is fixed to the rail, so it is just a matter of a slightly different Z height.
  2. It is not exactly 460 mm but 460.8 mm. Can I use it? Yes, the BLV X/Y system can handle even a 1.5 mm deviation. All you need to do is loosen the Y rail screws a bit and realign them to the new carbon tube. Very simple.
  3. My BLV carbon X-axis has oval holes on one side only. Why? I decided to make oval holes on one side only. This way the system is more reliable, yet flexible enough for the differences between builds.
  4. Some of the bottom holes are not sanded. To be honest, I'm a bit disappointed about that, since Mellow is a well-known, high-quality manufacturer. I think they rushed and shipped the last few pieces without a quality check because of the Chinese holiday. You can easily fix it, though. Be careful with the sharp carbon fibers: wear good gloves and sand the edges of the hole with a small file. It's very easy and takes only a couple of minutes.

I also received 3 reports of quality issues (over-sanding, damaged corners). I asked Mellow about it, and he immediately offered to send replacements. Quality is very important to him. Overall I'm very happy with the results, and to everyone who has already received the new BLV carbon X-axis: enjoy it.

docs.title: Orbiter V2 and Trianglelab Rapido
docs.text:
I started testing a few hotend-extruder setups, and I wanted to share my first impressions. So far I have tested Mellow's NF-Sunrise, which has done an amazing job. Then I tried a new setup: the LDO Orbiter V2 combined with the Trianglelab Rapido hotend. Without a doubt, Robert's new Orbiter V2 by LDO is fantastic. Just don't forget to readjust the hobbed wheel. I loved that it came with all the needed instructions, including Marlin, Klipper and RRF settings. Well done!

Mine came with the filament sensor. I printed the part needed for it, and I must say I absolutely love the design. I managed to get uniform layers without problems, even at very high speeds.

As for the Trianglelab Rapido, it's a really good hotend. With the Bondtech CHT nozzle I was able to print at 300 mm/s and still get impressive results on detailed models, as you can see below.

However, the Rapido became a bit redundant after E3D set a really low price for their new Revo Six/Micro: £69.90 on pre-order, compared to $90 for the Rapido. I tried swapping nozzles on the Rapido a couple of times. It went great until filament residue got stuck in the internal thread and prevented me from tightening the nozzle properly. It took me quite some time to clean the filament out, but in the end I was able to use it again.

Stay tuned. I will publish a new post about a few more setups I'm testing.

Sincerely,

Ben Levi

docs.title: Duet 3 6HC board
docs.text:
For a long time I have been fantasizing about buying the Duet 3 to use as the board for my BLV mgn Cube 3D printer. The Duet 3 6HC is the new generation of the well-known Duet WiFi board, running RepRap Firmware 3. It has all the hottest features, excellent specifications and the best documentation you could wish for in a 3D printer board. The main features are:

  • Fast 32-bit processor
  • High-speed bus for a Raspberry Pi (SBC)
  • 6 x Trinamic TMC5160 stepper drivers
  • 10 PWM outputs
  • 9 IO ports for endstops, probes and sensors
  • 4 thermistor or PT1000 inputs
  • 2 CAN-FD buses for expansion boards (up to 24 steppers)
  • Built-in Ethernet port
  • Duet Web Control interface and RRF3 firmware

There is much more, but these are the main points.

docs.title: So where's the problem?
docs.text: $225, not including shipping, is a lot of money, at least for me. Given my needs and the insane price, the Duet 3 just wasn't an option, and that's a shame.

docs.title: Finally
docs.text: All this was true until FYSETC decided to produce the Duet 3 6HC. Remember that the Duet 3 is open source. When I saw the Duet 3 6HC listing on AliExpress, I was excited, because I realized there was now another source for the Duet 3 6HC at a price that made it attractive to me. $145 for one of the best 3D printer boards on the market is just amazing, and that's $80 less. Shortly after I saw the listing, it was already deep in my order list and I started counting the days.

docs.title: Unboxing
docs.text:
I ordered the Duet 3 6HC and, out of curiosity, also the 3HC expansion board. The boards came well packed, wrapped in an antistatic bubble bag and a carton box. I must point out that they did a good job and included everything needed to install both the mainboard and the expansion board. For some reason, nowhere is it stated what comes with the board, so I prepared a complete list of all the components I received:

  • Duet 3 6HC clone board
  • Pack of 2.54mm Molex KK connectors and shells for most of the components
  • Pack of BVH-21T-P1.1B (JST) connectors and shells for steppers and heaters
  • Crimping pins for the high current connectors
  • 0.5m CAN cable
  • 16GB SD card for the Raspberry Pi (if you are using one)
  • 8GB SD card for the firmware and config
  • Raspberry Pi cable

As someone who has seen quite a few boards, I can say that this is a high-quality PCB. All components were properly soldered, and the board was properly washed and tested. The connectors provided by FYSETC are among the best I have ever worked with. Using this cheap SN-28B crimping tool, I got really nice crimps, better than on my original old Duet.

Before fixing the board to the back panel, I recommend updating the Duet 3 and making sure the firmware runs properly. You can find all the information you need about updating to the latest version in the Duet 3D documentation. The latest firmware can be downloaded from the RepRapFirmware releases page.

I had to drill new holes in the rear panel, since the Duet 3 6HC is much bigger than the old Duet WiFi. So it is worth checking that there is enough space on the back panel. For your convenience, here is a basic wiring diagram of the board as I installed it. Note that I haven't added the power button yet. Also, in this version I used an inductive sensor and an AC heated bed.

And this is what it looks like after installation:

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Before the board arrived, I sat down and read most of the Duet 3 documentation, and I highly recommend you do the same. It is all available in the Duet 3D documentation. For your convenience, I prepared a basic config you can start from when configuring your own system. Note that this config uses the new BIQU H2 extruder, so the endstop and probe locations should be changed according to your BLV Cube 3D printer settings.

My Duet 3 configuration files are included in the BLV mgn Cube project files, in the Firmware/Duet 3 folder (Basic Duet3 6HC config by Ben Levi.zip).

You can also check out David Husolo's Duet RRF3 configurations on his GitHub for both the BLV AM8 and the BLV mgn Cube. I would like to take this opportunity to thank David for his tremendous efforts in the community.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
I guess a lot of people are asking themselves whether it is worth upgrading to the Duet 3 6HC. After all, the Duet 3 6HC will function almost exactly like the old Duet WiFi, which costs less. That was true until FYSETC put their Duet 3 up for sale for $145, about $80 less than the official Duet. In terms of features, since the Duet 3 has a more powerful processor and double precision floating point, I allowed myself not to rely on the TMC drivers' auto interpolation and set my own micro-step settings. Keep in mind that with auto interpolation the driver will rarely reach 256 microsteps. If we force it to use a higher number of microsteps, it provides quieter motion, higher accuracy and fantastic print quality. The TMC5160 keeps surprising me with every print.

Those of you who use 3 Z axes for auto leveling will be happy to hear that the Duet 3 has 6 stepper drivers. That means you no longer need an expansion card for 3-axis auto leveling. The only downside of the Duet 3 for me is the lack of a WiFi module. True, a wireless module is slower than the Duet 3's Ethernet cable, but it's much more convenient.

After testing it for more than a month, I can say with complete confidence that overall I am very pleased with the board. Without a doubt, it is one of the best boards I have ever worked with. The prints come out great, and Duet's fantastic web interface has become a must-have feature for me. Recommended!

Here are some sample prints made with the Duet 3 6HC board.

Printed using the BIQU H2 direct drive extruder.

Filament: Noulei silk PLA filament and Prusament PLA Galaxy Silver.

I hope you enjoyed reading.

Sincerely,

Ben Levi

Edit: Unfortunately, I received requests to delete this post. Some people in the industry think that open source is not really open source, but a way to double their money. Sorry, but thanks to open source, even the average person can afford an Arduino, for example. I will make this clear again: my main goal is to make it all affordable for everyone. My sincere apologies to everyone who disagrees. In addition, some claimed that I may have received the board for free. I'm sorry, but I paid for it like anyone else, as the photo below shows.

docs.title: Let there be COB LED light
docs.text:
After a long time using an LED strip to light the print area, I wondered how I could make the LEDs sexier and hidden, without having to print parts. I was also tired of the uneven light shining through the diffuser because of the large gap between one LED and the next.

So I started researching again and finally found another type of LED strip that is more suitable for the BLV mgn Cube 3D printer: the COB LED strip.

In a COB strip the light-emitting diodes are much smaller than in a standard LED strip, which allows many more of them to fit on the strip. A standard LED strip has about 60 LEDs per meter, whereas a COB strip has 360 LEDs per meter. That is 6 times more than a standard strip, and it makes uniform light diffusion possible. Another advantage is that the LEDs are covered with a layer of silicone that acts as a diffuser and helps distribute the light evenly.

The smaller diodes also allow the strip to be narrower. I chose an 8 mm width, which let me insert the COB strip into the extrusion channel easily. The COB strip can be cut every 50 mm, and the light intensity can be adjusted too.

The first two strips I ordered from different stores on AliExpress disappointed me, and I almost gave up. Eventually I found a reliable store that sells quality COB strips. From the listing options I chose 6000K Cool White, 24V 360 LEDs and 2 meters. The strips came well packaged, met the specifications and felt like high-quality COB strips.

I cut the COB strip to the right length with scissors, following the markings (every 50 mm), and soldered on two 26 AWG wires. If you can't or don't want to solder, you can use this quick connector (choose the "For 8 mm PCB" option). Then I threaded the strip easily into the upper aluminum extrusion channels. The wires can be connected in 2 ways:

  • Direct connection to a 24V PSU
  • Duet fan output - if you connect the COB strip to a fan output, you can control its intensity with a slider in the Duet control panel

In my case I'm using FYSETC's amazing Duet 3 6HC board, so I had to define the lights as a fan output by adding these lines to the config.g file:

M950 F2 C"out9" Q500
M106 P2 S0.2 H-1 C"Lights"

Then I connected the COB LED strip wires to the OUT9 port on the Duet 3 6HC board.

I am very pleased with the end result. The lighting is very efficient, it looks good and I can control its intensity from the panel. I could not have asked for anything better. I really hope this helps those of you who want to add lighting to your printer.

In these pictures you can see the strips I installed. By the way, the prints in them were made with BIQU's amazing H2 extruder.

docs.title: Metal Kit II update and clearance sale
Metal Kit II update
docs.text:
It took 34 days to create this tiny part.

Over the course of those 34 days, I changed countless designs, tested, experimented, and gathered and analyzed data. Thanks to this small piece of the puzzle, I gained a better understanding of the entire picture.

To design a system that is truly optimized for performance and produces above-average print quality, I had to stop compromising. Since I still have access to academic articles through my old university student account, I started searching for information that could help me develop a better motion system. While I studied all sorts of belt drive principles, some of which were completely new to me, I also planned my experiments. At first, most experiments aimed to compare the old system with the prototypes. But in the process, I discovered that many clones do not even meet 30% of the specifications in the original datasheets. Since a user may accidentally pick a less reliable alternative, I had to replace every component. Rather than testing only 3 types of parts, I ended up buying and testing at least 28 different kinds of bearings, idlers, steppers, belts and more.

This is a great opportunity to thank a friend of mine who provided me with professional laboratory equipment. Half a year's salary would not cover most of it. Since he could be fired for this, no names or photos will be shared here. Thanks a lot, bud :)

So as not to bore you with too much data, here is an example of a small test. I built a closed-loop jig to find the correlation between vibration and bearing type.

The jig consists of a closed-loop belt, a stepper, a pulley, an idler, lab equipment for 3-axis vibration measurement with 3 probes plus a stationary pre-calibrated probe, 2 optical speed sensors for the steppers and idlers, a data logger and more. Each idler/bearing was tested with five mounting options, three types of belts, many bearings, Chinese idlers and Gates idlers. Isolating the idler vibrations was the most challenging part, and this was only one of many experiments. I also had to test each setup twice to measure both idler/bearing orientations (side and top).

Based on the information I gathered, I came to the following conclusions:

  • Structure. Despite its small size, this part aligns the two most critical parts of the system. You can see that it is attached to the frame in three different directions while aligning the profiles that hold the Y axis (second image). There are better ways to align a motion system frame, but given the circumstances and a DIY budget, this is the most efficient method.
  • No more idlers. They failed over and over again. My tests showed that even the original Gates idler for 9mm belts failed. Within 65 hours of work, black powder appeared inside the Gates bearings and the vibration levels increased. I have tested idlers/bearings from 28 manufacturers (with different clearances and accuracy levels) and have lost all trust in idlers.
  • Belt teeth on a bearing. The community has never given a definitive answer on whether belt teeth can run on bearings. There will always be different opinions, but I'm looking for facts, not opinions. As I write this, a small 680mm belt system test jig has been running (almost non-stop) for 384 hours. After only two checks, it has already answered 60% of my questions.

  • No tensioners, at least not like the traditional ones. A tensioner makes it very convenient to maintain the belt, but there are usually two or three moving parts with clearance between them. Whether it is held with a screw or locked with set screws, I measured a 19% increase in system noise. I have come up with a solution that I will share with you later.
  • Screws are not accurate. A large clearance between the screw's OD and the bearing/idler ID can also hurt the reliability of the system, and that is exactly the case when screws are used as idler/bearing axles. Shoulder bolts (-0.005h) are an option, but after measuring a couple of them, I found that some don't follow DIN specifications and their makers don't care about the customer. I think BOSSARD makes the best ones, but they are expensive. To solve this problem, I chose a high-precision custom solution.
  • Balance is crucial! Motion systems suffer from incorrect use of washers and from shafts/dowels of poor accuracy. It can even damage the belts. So I had to design parts that compress the bearings and also align them with the other components.
  • Weight and center of mass. Even light components matter, because of their position relative to the moving masses. Many changes there :)

This is just the tip of the iceberg. I have already changed many parts in the final design to make it more reliable. To those asking when it will be ready: I will probably send a few prototype files for manufacturing (not the full motion system). You can probably expect some of the parts to be revealed along the way, as I won't be able to hold back.

This is a way of "moving" the board indicator LEDs to the front without any soldering. The Duet WiFi board has a number of indicator LEDs for the heated bed, endstops, power, diag, status and more.

I think I found a simple, clean and fast way to "move" the LEDs to the front using cheap audio optical cable ($3 for 10m). So I ordered 20m of optical cable, started modeling some concept parts, and guess what? It worked!

Here is how I made this concept:

docs.title: PID tuning: important
docs.text:
I know that most of you are familiar with PID tuning and have already done it. But this is for those who have not performed a PID calibration yet.

PID calibration is a crucial step for getting high-quality prints. PID is an algorithm that uses 3 defined values to control and stabilize the nozzle and bed temperatures. The process is very simple. It should be done after building the printer and every time you change a component such as the heating element, the sensor, the bed sheet, or even when you add a silicone sock. At least 4 people asked for my help on Messenger, and most of their print quality issues vanished after a PID calibration.

Here are a few links with useful information about it:

  1. Duet3D documentation on tuning the heater temperature control
  2. BeTrue3D guide to PID tuning the hotend on a Duet WiFi/Ethernet
  3. If you are using Marlin: RepRap wiki on PID tuning

Please note:

  • Before running PID, the hotend and bed must be cool. Turn the printer off for half an hour before you start.
  • Before running PID on the hotend, heat the bed to your regular print temperature, position the hotend about 5mm above the bed, set the layer fan to your usual fan speed, and only then start the hotend PID.
  • Before running PID on the bed, turn on the hotend and the fan, and position the hotend about 10-20mm above the bed.

docs.title: BIQU H2 extruder review
docs.text: After a whole month of carefully testing the BIQU H2 extruder on my BLV mgn Cube 3D printer, I feel pretty confident writing my conclusions about BIQU's new H2 extruder. I promise you that I have tried hard to write a balanced and honest review. After all, no one pays me to write anything.

docs.title: So why is everyone excited about the new extruder?
docs.text:
Well, the BIQU H2 extruder actually resembles the E3D Hemera extruder, only with a smaller stepper and a higher gear ratio, at half the weight of the Hemera. Looking at the H2 extruder, it is clear that the main principle behind its design was to produce a direct drive at the lowest possible weight. Here is a picture that shows how small the H2 extruder is compared to the Trianglelab Matrix that I reviewed before:

Sure, I guess you can find a number of DIY extruders under 170g. But how many of them are actually made of aluminum and will survive inside the enclosure? And how many will not wear out fast because they are not made of printed parts? Anyway, I'm glad someone saw the potential and managed to reach such an impressive specification. And speaking of the specification:

BIQU H2 specs:

  • Direct drive extruder, ratio 7:1, torque 770mN.m
  • Size: 60x35x35mm
  • Weight: 219g including hotend and fan (mine was 225g)
  • Max pushing force: 7.5kg (I was only able to verify 4.62kg)
  • Max temperature: 260ºC, upgradeable to 500ºC
  • NEMA14 1.8º stepper motor
  • Nominal e-steps: 932 steps/mm for a 16x setup (after calibration: 917.444)
  • NTC 3950 100k thermistor and a 24V heater

It wasn't cheap. $100 for the extruder is definitely expensive. But when I bought it, there was no reliable direct drive alternative that weighed less than the H2. If there were alternatives in serial production, I guess the price would have been much lower. After a rather short wait, the package arrived and I was very excited to open it. The extruder came in an airtight custom box, lying comfortably in a soft material that kept it from being damaged. Very neat. It came with instructions and a separate bag that contained all the other accessories and tools. Inside the package you will find:

  • BIQU H2 extruder
  • 3510 24V fan with a long cable
  • 35mm fan grill
  • NTC 3950 100k thermistor
  • 24V 40W heater with thick cable insulation
  • Stepper motor cable
  • Heat block silicone sock
  • Yellow duck (my favorite item in this order)
  • Screws and tools
  • Additional order: all-metal heatbreaks for higher temperature printing, 1 x 303 stainless steel heatbreak and 1 x titanium heatbreak

I must say I was very impressed with the build quality of the extruder. Everything is made of aluminum and looks good. The parts have been smoothed, with no chips, no dirt and no visual defects. I was sure the gears were made of glass-filled plastic, but I was pleasantly surprised when I realized they were actually metal gears. However, I found some issues that bothered me a lot, and I had to fix them before the first use. Below you can read more about the changes I made. Here are some pictures of the extruder before I started disassembling and testing it.

This is what it looks like after removing the fan and exposing the entire 7:1 gear mechanism:

The heat block of the extruder is actually a regular aluminum heat block from which large pieces were shaved and drilled out, probably to save weight. The heatbreak is a standard size but has a D profile, and it is locked with two set screws. The first photo shows the all-metal heatbreaks. In the last photo, I tried a regular heat block and it worked fine.

Before you assemble the heat block, I recommend calibrating your extruder e-steps. I found a huge difference between BIQU's recommended e-steps (932) and the calibrated e-steps for my H2 extruder (917.444). This is also a good moment to check that the motor direction is correct.

One of the first modifications I made was to change the direction of the heat block. I wanted the narrow part to face the front of the printer so I could use an efficient cooling solution. I also didn't like the inner finish of the original BIQU nozzle (first photo), so I replaced it with an amazing quality nozzle that I had purchased from Mellow's store. To lock the nozzle in place, I used a wrench and inserted an Allen key into the heater hole. This way I tightened the nozzle without damaging the exterior finish of the block (second photo).

After changing the heat block orientation and the nozzle, I started taking care of something else that was bothering me. I may be wrong, but it seems that the gears are made of black coated steel that can rust over time due to moisture in the air. I also noticed that BIQU doesn't grease the gears before sending them out to customers, and I found that very disturbing. Applying a little grease to the gear system makes it work better, helps the gears last longer and protects them from moisture in the long run. Luckily, I had ordered the SuperPINDA from Prusa to test its accuracy against the mini IR sensor, and I added 5 pcs of Prusa grease to that order. I found it to be an excellent grease, even for linear rails. So I spread out a piece of paper, carefully disassembled the gears and gently greased all the components. When greasing the gears, take care not to grease the wheels that pull the filament. Any oil on them can cause an extrusion failure.

Immediately after assembling everything, I had to disassemble it all again because I found another annoying issue. A cable must be connected to the extruder stepper motor, and someone chose to assemble the H2 motor so that the cable socket faces down. That is a critical mistake. At some point the cable may come loose, get stuck in the part you are printing and destroy the whole print. To fix it, disassemble the extruder and take out the two tiny M3 screws that fix the extruder body to the stepper motor. Rotate the stepper motor 180 degrees and tighten the screws again. Please mind that the threads are short and can be easily stripped, so screw them in gently and not too tight.

After several hours of design work and simulations, I was able to get a bracket strong enough to support the H2 extruder that also fits the metal kit of my BLV mgn Cube 3D printer. Please note that I added spring washers to the long H2 extruder screws. After a few dozen hours of printing, I noticed that I had to re-tighten the long screws that hold all the H2 components together, and adding spring washers fixed the issue completely. I did a number of tests using dual 3510 ball bearing blowers, but the airflow was just ridiculously weak. I ended up using a powerful dual ball bearing 5015 blower fan, which gave me fantastic results. Feel free to download the bracket files. I included both the STL file and the STEP (CAD) file, so you can easily make changes as you wish:

The bracket is included in the BLV mgn Cube project files: the STL files are in STL files to print/Biqu H2 extruder adapter For Metal kit and the STEP files are in open source/Biqu H2 adapter For Metal kit.

The files are licensed under the Creative Commons - Attribution - Non-Commercial - Share Alike license.

I always like to install thermistors and heaters at the end of the process, as they are very sensitive and the thin cables can tear easily. I don't compromise on thermistor reading quality, so I replaced the H2's original NTC 3950 100k thermistor with a higher quality Semitec 104NT-4-R025H42G thermistor. I also replaced the heater with the stable 40W heater that I always use. I'm also waiting for Mellow's new 70W ceramic heater to come back in stock, and I'll probably be one of the first to order it for testing. Don't forget to apply non-conductive thermal paste to both the heater and the thermistor. This helps stabilize the temperature and gives more accurate readings.

And of course, every block and nozzle gets the Slice Engineering protective coating, which has already saved me a few hotends in the past. It creates a polymer layer that isolates the block and makes it easy to clean. Together with the original silicone sock, the hotend is much safer now.

Small note: the coating will not make your heat block non-stick like PTFE, but it will be really easy to remove filament from the block. Over time, your block will not get that disgusting color from burnt filament residue. Despite the small amount of liquid, it was already enough for 12 nozzles and I still had 25% of the bottle left.

I almost forgot to mention that I replaced the mini IR sensor, which was damaged by a curious child ("Dad, I touched this and it's not lit anymore..."), with an inductive auto leveling sensor. I placed it on the back of the X carriage (the bracket is also included in the H2 bracket zip). I added a 50mm M3 screw on top of the X carriage and secured all the wires to it with a zip tie. Then I used this 13mm expandable cable sleeve for the cables.

Now, hold on a second before you load filament into your H2 extruder. It turns out BIQU left the filament opening exposed, so the filament will probably rub against the edge of the hole. To solve the problem, I added a pneumatic connector. It slightly increases the weight but prevents the filament from grinding on the hole edges.

With all the preparations done, I loaded a new spool of silk rainbow PLA that I really like and started testing.

docs.title: Sample tests
docs.text: For a whole month I abused the extruder and pushed it to the limit. I started by feeding almost 500g of PLA through it without printing, just to check for filament residue in the gear assembly. I heated the extruder to simulate an enclosure and checked for missed steps. With the BIQU H2 I printed almost 5 spools of filament: PLA, silk PLA, TPU, PETG and a PC blend using the all-metal heatbreak. Take your time and look at my print samples:

docs.title: Final conclusion
docs.text:
Yes, it is expensive and there are many things to improve, but I would buy it again. My experience with the H2 extruder was very good. The extrusion is very consistent, and in most of my prints the layers were uniform. The pushing force is good, it handles most filament types well, and it's well built, light and reliable. It is not easy to reassemble, but that's not something you do every day. Currently, there are not many mass-produced competitors that can deliver the same results at such a low weight. Personally, I am less excited about extruders that have printed parts in the gear assembly, so for me this is the only alternative. I hope BIQU will read this review and maybe address some of the issues. I also think there is room to reduce its weight even further.

Get the BIQU H2 extruder on AliExpress.

Ben Levi

docs.title: Trianglelab Matrix adapter for the Metal Kit
docs.text:
For a long time I have been considering whether to buy the E3D Hemera extruder. To my great joy, a new extruder from Trianglelab appeared: the Matrix. It is identical to the Hemera in most of its properties, but it costs much less and is still high quality.

The main reasons I wanted to try the Matrix so much are:

  • Short filament path. The distance between the drive wheels and the nozzle is 26mm. This is a huge advantage when printing soft and flexible materials. Beyond that, the retraction distance is significantly smaller (mine is set to 0.6mm). A much lower value can also be used for the pressure advance feature in RepRap Firmware, which means more accurate extrusion and faster printing.
  • Bi-metal heatbreak. The heatbreak tube is made of two different materials with different thermal conductivity. This creates very efficient thermal separation compared to other extruders, and an excellent buffer between the heat block and the part that should always stay cold: the dual gears that push the filament in.

I'm not even counting the dual gear drive with a 1:3 gear ratio and the other features, because they have almost become standard. The only downside of this setup is the weight. For me, the total weight of the hotend and extruder was about 360 grams. It is heavier than other extruders, but on the other hand, the performance can be very surprising.

As you can see, I was immediately tempted and bought the new Matrix extruder. After using it for a pretty long time on my BLV mgn Cube 3D printer (upgraded with the Metal Kit), I feel quite comfortable writing an objective opinion about it.

The new extruder came well packaged, with all components in separate bags marked with detailed stickers. A page listing the entire contents of the package was also included, with a QR code that leads to a neat assembly guide. They even added a Matrix STEP (CAD) file in case anyone wants to model mounts and extras. I must note that Trianglelab always includes all the necessary components with their products, as well as detailed instructions. Everything is included, whether it's heat shrinks, adapters, wires or just zip ties. Well done!

This is what it looks like shortly before mounting it on the X axis:

docs.title: Print test
docs.text: I guess by now you already want to see some print results. So for those who can't resist, here are some pictures of objects printed with the Trianglelab Matrix extruder. By the way, I really like printing this cube. It's quite funny that it comes out more accurate when printed on a BLV printer.

docs.title: Installing the extruder
docs.text:
Although the Matrix is very similar to the Hemera, the dimensions are slightly different, so I preferred to design an adapter for the BLV Metal Kit. When I designed the adapter, I focused on the nozzle position and tried to find the optimal location. Some of the considerations were keeping a proper center of gravity and not losing build plate area.

The Matrix adapter is available in the download section below. I also uploaded the source file (STEP file), so you can easily add features and make changes as you wish. To assemble the adapter, you will need the following components:

  • BLV mgn Cube 3D printer with the Metal Kit upgrade
  • BLV Matrix adapter, printed in PETG/ASA/ABS with 80%+ infill
  • Trianglelab Matrix extruder
  • 3 x M3 8mm hex flat head screws
  • 1 x M3 16mm hex flat head screw
  • 2 x M3 8mm hex socket head screws
  • 3 x M3 16mm hex socket head screws
  • 3 x M3 washers

Follow these instructions to assemble the adapter:

docs.title: Layer fan
docs.text: For now I chose to use a James Tongue fan duct as the layer fan, but I modified the bracket to fit the Trianglelab Matrix extruder so the nozzle sits right in the middle. The modified fan mount is available in the download section below.

docs.title: Download section
docs.text:
The adapter and the fan adapter are included in the BLV mgn Cube project files: the STL files are in STL files to print/Trianglelab Matrix adapter For Metal kit and the STEP files are in open source/Trianglelab Matrix adapter for Metal kit.

File description:

  • BLV matrix adapter for metal kit.step - adapter source file
  • BLV matrix adapter for metal kit.stl - the Matrix adapter file to print
  • BLV matrix fan adapter.step - fan mount source file
  • BLV matrix fan adapter.stl - if you are using the James Tongue fan bracket, print this file

docs.title: Firmware changes (RRF3)
docs.text:
To use the Matrix, you have to change the following lines in the config.g file on your Duet. Please mind that these lines are for RRF3.

  • Thermistor: change the thermistor settings to match the Matrix thermistor. In the M308 line, change the T, B and C values to: T107537 B4725 C7.06e-8
  • E-steps: for me, the default e-steps from the Trianglelab manual were wrong, so I calibrated my Matrix extruder to find the most accurate setting. I advise you to calibrate your extruder too. I had to change the e-steps value in the M92 line to: E324.214
  • Stepper driver: invert your extruder drive direction by changing the S value to S0 or S1 in the M569 line.
  • Probe position: for the mini IR sensor, the offset values in the G31 line are: X16.795 Y25.4

Important: re-calibrate your Z offset right after changing the hotend.

docs.title: Final conclusion
docs.text:
My personal experience with the new Matrix extruder has been very positive. I highly recommend it to anyone who wants an all-in-one extruder package. Although it is quite heavy, you get consistent extrusion, short retractions and an excellent printing experience. If I could change anything, I would start with a smaller stepper, such as a NEMA14, combined with a higher gear ratio. But overall, I really like it.

Note: I will probably test the BIQU H2 extruder (219g) with its 7:1 gear ratio next.

Get the Trianglelab Matrix extruder on AliExpress.
