docs.title: Unboxing: the FYSETC BLV mgn Cube full kit
docs.text:
This time they caught me by surprise.

A friend of mine (@Harel) contacted FYSETC after having difficulty ordering a kit from Blurolls. It turns out someone there took his request very seriously and made a new, truly complete BLV mgn Cube full kit. When he finally got his new kit, he asked me to build the BLV Cube 3D printer for him. I usually don't have free time, but he asked so nicely that I agreed. Less than two hours later he arrived, handed me two packages with a total weight of over 30kg and smiled. Well, he had a reason to smile.

I waited for the evening, the kids fell asleep, and I could finally sink into what I really love.

Nothing prepared me for what came next.

A few moments after I spread the contents of the cartons on the floor, I stood there overwhelmed for a few minutes. I could not believe my eyes and kept mumbling "It's all there..."

There is no other explanation: someone there actually did their homework, and did it well.

Someone at FYSETC built the printer down to the last detail, tested it properly, assembled all the right parts, simplified the wiring diagram for easy installation, added an ingenious Neopixel kit to the front panel, and updated and upgraded most of the printer components into an almost perfect kit.

Without a doubt, this kit can save up to 60% of the printer building time.

Kudos to those who were responsible for creating the new BLV mgn Cube kit, well done!

docs.title: The kit
docs.text:
You can see they cared about everything, starting with the strict packaging. All screws are well labeled, and all wiring is pre-crimped or comes with a plug, ready for installation without any soldering or crimping. The SSR has its own pre-crimped wires, and so do all the other components, even the motors. The motor cables are labeled and their wires are arranged in the correct order, ready to use. They added a carbon sticker for the panels, and each screw hole has a countersink so the sticker will hide it. They added the insulation pads and even an adhesive tape for them. They used the new Blind Joints frame for a quick frame installation and upgraded the power supply to a Mean Well 600W (from 450W). They added installation tools and even made sure the linear rails have red caps that prevent the carriage from falling off during installation. And yes, the rails run smoothly. You can choose an all-metal throat or a PTFE throat. It's all there, and much more.

The most amazing part is that they took all the hassle involved in installing the Neopixel rings and turned it into an installation of less than a minute. Even my 5-year-old kid could install it in less than a minute. They also replaced the mini IR sensor with a BLTouch and added a BuildTak glass, among many other things.

I have to stop here.

It can't be that everything is so perfect. True, not everything is perfect. I wish the extrusions were better packed, since a few of them came slightly scratched. Also, they used the old 5015 fan setup for the hotend, while I have since added an improved cooling part using dual 4010 blowers. The kit also doesn't include the Metal Kit, which is my favorite choice over the printed parts. I have just completed the parts testing phase, including testing the boards and motors, bearing tolerances and rail motion. Overall I am very pleased. Next I will probably build the frame, and as soon as the Metal Kit arrives I will continue building the new BLV mgn Cube 3D printer kit. Right now the kit looks promising and I hope I will not be disappointed. I'm afraid my friend may not get his printer back.

Before you start reading, here are all the relevant links:

  • The new FYSETC BLV mgn Cube 3D printer kit (cheaper shipping is planned, as they shipped to their US and ES warehouses)
  • The FYSETC BLV GitHub project (firmware, docs and wiring)
  • The BLV mgn Cube FYSETC kit full wiring diagrams
  • The BLV mgn Cube Metal Kit (replaces all the printed parts with metal parts)
  • The modified FYSETC STL files for the BLV mgn Cube printer

docs.title: The frame
docs.text:
Before I even opened the smaller box, I could guess the frame was in it from the weight and the noise the box made when I lifted it. As soon as I opened the box, I noticed that most of the profiles were protected with a thick layer of nylon, and there was foam to protect the contents of the box. Despite this, a few extrusions were slightly scratched, but these were minor, almost unnoticeable scratches.

I measured all the profiles and found that they were all very accurate. The drilled holes were accurate but slightly unclean, and I had to clean out some aluminum chips left inside.

What are Blind Joints?

The frame comes as a Blind Joints setup, which allows you to assemble the frame without brackets. It saves over 80% of the assembly time. All it takes is screwing in the provided button screw and sliding the screw head into the channel of the other extrusion, as shown in the video. Also check out our community member Harel's Blind Joints frame assembly video.

Inside the box I also found a huge plastic bag with lots of small bags inside. Each bag was tagged and contained a certain type of screw. The number of screws was accurate in most cases, and some bags even had spares. I was surprised to find parts I did not include in the original BLV mgn Cube 3D printer BOM, like the couplings (standoffs) for fixing the mainboard to the rear composite panel, not to mention the flat head screws for the outer composite panels.

Overall I am very pleased with the frame extrusions, even before building the entire frame.

docs.title: Mainboard and LCD
docs.text:
As in the original BOM of the project, the kit comes with an excellent clone of the Duet 2 WiFi board, one of the best and most reliable boards running RepRap. Even though the newer Duet 3 is out, the Duet 2 is still one of the most recommended boards. It meets the needs of 3D printers and doesn't fall short of its bigger, newer and more expensive brother in many parameters. It is also worth mentioning that the Duet family is the most documented board family on the internet. The board in the kit is the latest hardware version, v1.04. It came well packed together with all the necessary accessories: a USB cable, an SD card with basic firmware, driver heatsinks, pins, plugs and jumpers.

The board came with a 5" PanelDue V3.0 touch LCD, an even larger screen than the one in the original BOM. The new 5" screen will not fit the original printed BLV mgn Cube front panel, so FYSETC uploaded all the new files needed to support it. They are available as modified STL files on Thingiverse. I really like that they took it seriously and decided to customize the parts and upload the STLs to Thingiverse.

The kit's wiring diagram:

docs.title: BMG geared dual-drive extruder
docs.text:
The extruder in the kit is the BMG geared 1:3 dual-drive extruder. It's a clone of the $80 Bondtech BMG extruder, and to be honest, the clone is way better than the original Bondtech.

Unlike the original Bondtech, which is made with MJF 3D printing, the clone is produced by plastic injection molding, which is more precise and rigid, not to mention the cheap price. I also checked the hobbed gear wheels, and they align perfectly on the filament. Inside the plastic bag were the tools needed for installation, 2 clips, a PTFE tube and screws.

docs.title: Stepper motors
docs.text:
I must admit they did a fantastic job here. The motors were placed inside an EPE foam package, each in its own place, and each motor was labeled to prevent confusion during installation. I also found a nylon bag in the kit with all the motor cables. All cable ends were ready for installation with a suitable plug, which saves a lot of frustration. Each cable was labeled, so you know where it needs to connect, and each cable had the exact length for its axis: the Z and extruder cables were long and the X/Y cables were short, as needed. I was surprised to find out later that even the wire order was correct, so there is no need to swap motor wires to get the right motor directions. Well done, FYSETC!

I noticed that the kit motors come from a different manufacturer than the one specified in the BOM. I wanted to make sure they matched the specs, but when I searched for data by model number I found nothing. Apparently this is a special production run for FYSETC, so I contacted them and they sent me the motor datasheets. According to the datasheets, they are pretty similar to the stepper motors I originally recommended. Even though I know they tested them on a working BLV Cube 3D printer, I will only have a solid opinion about the motors after building the kit and testing it myself.

  • Extruder: 1 x 42SHDC4038Z-22B
  • Z axis: 2 x 42SHDC6037Z-24B
  • Y/X axis: 2 x 42SHTNC6009Z-24B

For your convenience, here is the technical information for the motors:

Pictures of the labels and the different cable lengths:

docs.title: Teflon-coated leadscrews and POM TR8 nuts
docs.text: I really like this upgrade, mainly because I installed PTFE leadscrews on my Ender 3 V2 prototype (a new project) and they are really great, especially the POM TR8 nut. It's non-stick, heat resistant, and works great without any weird squeaking sounds. The quality is amazing, and you can see it for yourself even though I am not a professional photographer.

docs.title: PSU setup
docs.text:
This thing is huge! They managed to provide this 2kg beast, a genuine Mean Well SE-600-24 switching power supply rated at 24V, 25A and 600W (unlike the 450W PSU in the first kit). It's a very high-quality branded PSU that can cover all the BLV printer requirements.

Note: Before connecting the PSU, check whether it's set to 110V or 230V. The one I got was set to 230V, as it should be. If you live in the USA, switch it to 110V first.

As you could guess, they added all the necessary cables, including a power cord (with a dedicated hole in the panel), pre-crimped cables, buttons and an SSR module. Everything is easy to install without crimping any cables. Nice!

The FYSETC team also made a wiring diagram for the PSU:

docs.title: Auto leveling sensor: BLTouch
docs.text:
Because the kit has a BuildTak glass bed, the original IR optical sensor from the project's BOM cannot be used. Instead, they included a BLTouch sensor as the auto leveling sensor. It's not the original Antclabs sensor, but in my experience most of the updated clones give reliable results similar to the original BLTouch. It came with an extension cable of the right length.

Connecting the auto leveling sensor is very easy. Here is the diagram that shows how to connect it:

docs.title: Hotend setup
docs.text:
All the V6 hotend parts came bundled in one nylon bag. These parts are included:

  • Fully assembled E3D V6 hotend clone with a silicone sock
  • PTFE throat, already assembled
  • All-metal throat for high-temperature filaments
  • High-quality 0.4mm nozzle
  • Thermal compound, which may be needed if you use the all-metal throat
  • HT-NTC100K thermistor
  • 40W 24V heater

The hotend looks good and the inner throat surface looks quite smooth. I couldn't see any problem with it, but I would have preferred the heat block to have a polished finish.

They also included a flexible sleeve (Prusa style) and a PTFE tube with a 1.9mm ID.

docs.title: Outer panels and insulation
docs.text:
At first I didn't pay attention to the panels, since I thought, what could be new? Then I picked them up and immediately noticed that they are relatively heavy compared to other composite panels. Composite panels are also called "sandwich panels" or "ACP". These are flat panels made of two thin aluminum sheets bonded to a non-aluminum core. The panels in the kit have relatively thick aluminum sheets, and you can feel it. The panels are installed around the printer frame with screws. FYSETC made countersunk holes and added flat head screws for the panels. The idea is very nice because it allows the carbon sticker (also provided) to hide the screws. They also added screw holes for the board and all the electrical components, including the power plug. Note: Don't forget to peel off the protective layer.

Another interesting addition, which also appears in the BOM, is the acoustic insulation panels. They added double-sided adhesive tape for the installation.

Inside a thick cardboard tube I found a roll of quality carbon sticker for the outer panels. They also added a small plastic tool to help with the sticker installation, but because it was inserted into the tube, it warped, so I will have to use my own plastic card. Thank you for adding the carbon sticker.

docs.title: Heated bed and glass platform
docs.text:
The most sensitive part is the heated bed. It's a standard 4mm 410x310 aluminum heated bed with a built-in NTC 100K thermistor and silicone power cables. The cables have the right AWG and the correct length, and they are soldered to the bottom pads. The wire ends are pre-crimped and the thermistor wires already have a Duet plug installed. All of the bed cables are protected inside a Prusa-style flexible sleeve. The upper surface of the bed is covered with a protective nylon layer, which must be removed before use.

Since thin aluminum sheets tend to warp, they included a BuildTak glass branded with the printer name. How cool is that? The glass surface also has a protective nylon layer on top, which must be removed before use. The BuildTak glass ensures a relatively flat bed surface and quick part release after cooling. I'm still considering putting a magnetic surface and a spring steel sheet on the glass.

The kit also includes a thick adhesive thermal insulation layer that needs to be glued to the bottom of the heated bed, as you can see in the photos.

You are not mistaken, they really added 4 original Creality heated bed adjustment wheels, as well as the original yellow Creality CR-10 springs for the heated bed.

docs.title: Linear rails
docs.text:
The quality of the rails is directly related to the print quality. Although these are not HIWIN rails, I was deeply impressed by their quality. Unfortunately, even though I asked, they didn't reveal the source of the linear rails. I can understand that, since other Chinese stores would want to sell rails of this quality too. Anyway, back to the rails.

The linear rails came wrapped in sealed plastic bags. I was relieved to discover a red cap at each end of every rail. The cap prevents the carriage from falling off and scattering all the steel balls. Of course, you can remove the red caps later as needed.

I checked a few things while testing the linear rails:

  • How straight they are. I used a dial indicator and also the simple method of laying the rails on a flat surface and looking for light from below. All the rails were completely straight, with no distortion.
  • Smooth motion. All the rails, without exception, moved surprisingly smoothly. Unlike others, I don't measure how gravity affects the carriage, since that can indicate low tolerance. My indication is a time/force table for each rail, and they all passed.

Surprisingly, the rails were cut perfectly at the original factory, without the use of an abrasive saw. A clean cut usually indicates that these are new rails rather than second-hand ones.

The rail channels are very clean, with no sign of over-lubrication, and the rubber seals are clean and new.

I am definitely going to use them in the printer. Overall, these are excellent quality rails!

docs.title: BLV Neopixel controller
docs.text:
I think this was the thing I most wanted to see. The original BLV mgn Cube project translates the printer status into a light signal displayed on the front panel using Neopixel LED rings. But it required knowledge, soldering, flashing an Arduino and very complicated wiring. FYSETC made everything easy. How easy? So easy that my 5-year-old kid could put it all together in less than a minute, and it works right out of the box. How awesome is that!

Here is what the Neopixel kit contains:

  • 3 x Neopixel rings with a connector pre-soldered on the back
  • 1 x mainboard with an STM chip and an integrated voltage regulator suitable for 24V/12V
  • 3 x Neopixel cables with suitable plugs
  • 1 x data cable for getting the data from the Duet 2 WiFi board (not in the picture)
  • 1 x power cable to feed the controller board

You should have seen the happiness in my eyes when I connected everything and it just worked. In less than a minute everything was running without problems or glitches. Right after turning on the boards, all 3 Neopixel rings showed an animation and then the printer status. Amazing, and so simple!

Here you can see the wiring diagram and how to connect the Neopixel system. All the cables are ready to use, with no soldering needed.

  • First, plug the Neopixel cable into the Neopixel ring pins. The black wire should be connected to the "G" (ground) pin.

  • Then connect the 3 Neopixel cables to the bottom left sockets (3 pins).
  • Then connect the data cable (black and white wires) to the bottom right socket (2 pins).
  • Now connect the other end of the data cable (black and white wires) to the PanelDue socket on the Duet, as shown in the picture.
  • Connect the wide LCD cable to the back of the 5" LCD and to the left socket on the Duet.
  • Connect the power cable to the screw terminal (don't forget to trim the wire ends a bit).

And that's it. As simple as that!

docs.title: Cable management
docs.text: Here you can see some of the accessories, couplings and GT2 pulleys.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Yes, there are finally tools included in the kit as well. Well done!

docs.title: LED strips
docs.text: The kit comes with two 24V white LED strips that should fit perfectly into the original BLV mgn Cube diffusers. I liked that someone devoted time to measuring and preparing the LED strips. It saves us a lot of time, very nice.

docs.title: Endstops
docs.text:
Inside the kit you will also find two endstop switches with long cables. Please note that FYSETC made a few changes to the endstop mounts. Download the updated endstop mount STL on Thingiverse.

Check the wiring diagram to connect the endstops.

docs.title: Fans
docs.text: They included all the necessary 24V fans with the appropriate cable lengths, and each fan cable already has a suitable plug, ready to install. Some of you have noticed that there is a 5015 fan for part cooling. I have since upgraded the original part cooling to dual 4010 blower fans. You can still use the 5015 fan, but the dual 4010 blower fans are much more powerful.

docs.title: More parts
docs.text:
They added 6m of reinforced fiberglass GT2 Gates belts, high-quality bearings (excellent tolerance), a few brackets for the frame if needed (front panel extrusion), HEPA filters and even a brass brush to clean the hotend. Personally, I would use the brass brush only with an X nozzle or a hardened steel nozzle. Using a brass brush to clean a brass nozzle damages the nozzle.

I'm a little exhausted after writing this unboxing review and preparing the pictures. I did not expect to like the FYSETC kit so much. A lot of thought has been put into it. Undoubtedly, the person who made the kit has built the printer and understood exactly what was needed.

Now I'm left with a huge problem: I don't know how to tell my friend that after I put it together, the printer will stay with me 😉

I promise to keep you updated during and after the build.

Yours,

Ben Levi

Disclaimer: I make no profit from any kits that are sold. This kit belongs to my friend, and the project is open source and non-profit.

docs.title: BLV mgn12 mod
docs.text:
For Anet A8 / Prusa i3

This project turns the Anet A8 into a precise 3D printer, with MGN12 rails mounted on an aluminum extrusion frame. With small changes it is compatible with Pheneeny's AM8 mod. The result is a much more reliable, accurate and faster printer.

Download all files Thingiverse Remixes Facebook group

docs.title: Why MGN rails
docs.text: Low and mid range printers usually move on linear bearings or Delrin wheels because they are cheaper than MGN rails, and the price is accuracy and reliability. MGN linear rails are stiffer, very precise and smooth. They allow faster printing without losing quality, and because the rails are fixed to the frame, they block unwanted motion from bent threaded rods or the other axes. That is why high-end printers use them. Affordable MGN rails on AliExpress made this upgrade possible.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Patience required. The MGN rails must be perfectly straight and aligned. Rushing this step causes problems later.
  • Source file. The STEP file is in the project ZIP. If you remix it, follow the license (CC BY-NC-SA) and mark your work as a remix.
  • Bed position. You may need to re-center the bed coordinates in Marlin, or move the Z extrusion to center the bed.
  • Simplify3D. A build plate for Simplify3D is available.
  • Share it. An "I made one" photo on Thingiverse or in the Facebook group is always appreciated.

docs.title: Mod variations
docs.text:
1. Anet A8 converted to AM8 (original 440 mm height) with the BLV mgn12 mod. If you already own an AM8 and want to keep its height, use 350 mm rails instead of 400 mm.

  2. Anet A8 converted to AM8 with a taller 500 mm Z axis and the BLV mgn12 mod. Build the AM8 with these changes:

    • instead of 2 × 440 mm 2040 extrusions → 2 × 500 mm (or longer) 2040 extrusions
    • instead of 2 × 340 mm 2040 extrusions → 4 × 364 mm 2040 extrusions
    • longer 400 mm threaded rods

    Not all the AM8 parts are needed. See what to print. 3. Anet AM8 freestyle with the BLV mgn12 mod. The parts are modular and can be fitted as you like. For a custom size with a bigger bed or a taller Z axis, choose the extrusion lengths and attach the parts to them.

Requirements

An Anet A8 (or a similar Prusa i3 style printer), the AM8 frame upgrade, basic technical skills, spare time and a mid-range budget.

docs.title: Rail tips
docs.text:
I started with affordable MGN12H rails from AliExpress at about $18 each. After buying from four different sellers, I found the best value at the CNA Mechanical Parts Store. Their carriages slide smoothly straight out of the box, with no cleaning needed. For higher quality at a reasonable price, the HIWIN rail set is excellent.

Sellers to avoid

Avoid RDC Official Store and linkcnc Store on AliExpress. linkcnc sent me a used, damaged rail that was shorter than ordered and stayed stuck even after cleaning. RDC started shipping carriages that don't match the MGN standard.

Cleaning and lubrication. New rails usually feel rough because they are coated with a protective oil at the factory. Clean it off (several YouTube videos show how to clean the carriage with WD-40), then lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or a PTFE silicone grease. These are miniature rails, so avoid thick grease. The goal is a smooth carriage without free play.

The video below shows the cleaning process well. Work over a container so you don't lose any steel balls. After reassembly there is room for one more ball, which is normal.

Tuning up cheap Chinese linear bearings

Mounting the rails takes patience. They must be perfectly straight and aligned, and rushing this step causes problems later.

Don't rely on the gravity test

Tilting a rail and watching the carriage slide down says nothing about its quality. A rail with too much free play passes easily and then fails every print quality test. The tolerance grade of the rail sets the friction of the carriage.

docs.title: BLV 3D printer enclosure: progress
docs.text:
The project beta has been released to the public.

I know many of you have been waiting for an update, so I can finally share it with you.

I announced on the BLV Facebook group that I had started developing a new universal extrusion system as part of the affordable BLV enclosure project, made for a wide range of 3D printers. The main reason I chose to develop the BLV enclosure is my dear wife. Our house is not that big, and as the number of printers grew, she thought they were really ugly and didn't suit the house. So I set out to create an enclosure with a modern, clean design, round lines and delicate contours. I have now received her official approval to place printers even in the living room 😍.

Designing a system like this requires experience in industrial design and production techniques, so the task was not easy. I wanted to create a reliable, modular system that is easy to assemble, affordable, and can be used with any 3D printer.

A small reminder of the original design concept sketch:

After hundreds of hours designing the new extrusion system and more than 12 different prototypes, I can finally reveal the progress of the BLV enclosure project. I received the latest version of the BLV enclosure prototype. The parts came in a heavy package, carefully wrapped in paper to protect them from damage during shipping. I was as excited as a little boy who had just received a birthday present.

As you can see, the entire enclosure is made of aluminum extrusion profiles and cast aluminum corners. Remember I said it's universal? Well, the enclosure is meant to suit any type of 3D printer. The only things that change are the length of the extrusion profiles, the panels, and the location of the cable and ventilation holes. Right after I removed all the packaging, this is what I saw:

Designing the corner component alone took almost three full months, but I don't regret the time I invested in developing this extrusion system. The quality of the parts is just amazing. It is not easy to produce parts of such high quality. I had to make a number of changes before I came up with this version, which quickly turned out to be a good prototype.

The profiles are very easy to assemble. Assembling the entire enclosure took no more than 15 minutes. Each extrusion profile fits snugly into the corner component and is locked with two set screws. Both the extrusion and the corner have a self-alignment feature that places them at the same height, creating a uniform and smooth look, so there is no need to waste time aligning the frame. Overall, the frame is extremely rigid, even though the whole structure consists of thin aluminum extrusions and plexiglass panels.

In the video below, you can see at 0:18 how the profiles connect:

A uniform and smooth look. If only you could imagine how long a road it was and how many prototypes I made until all the parts fit and aligned perfectly with each other, as shown in the pictures.

I am currently waiting for the door parts. I'm planning two doors, so it will be easy to use the printer, replace the filament and take out the printed object. The door is expected to have a magnetic lock mechanism and a clean look.

I made sure to use cast acrylic and not extruded acrylic. Cast acrylic is much clearer and has no defects compared to extruded acrylic, but it is more expensive. After the quick frame assembly, I realized that the panels were thinner than I planned: 2.7mm instead of 3mm, so they were a bit shaky. With the nylon protective film, the plexiglass is exactly 3mm thick, and it's more than perfect. Everything sits exactly as I planned. The structure is very strong, reliable and lightweight compared to other enclosures. I'm happy with the result.

In this version, I designed a hole for a low-RPM fan (needed when printing flexible materials). There is a dedicated cover that closes the hole for those who don't want a fan. I also added a rubber grommet for external cables. I accidentally installed the panel upside down, since the cable hole was supposed to be at the bottom. Some of the hive walls broke during shipping, so the next design will have a thicker hive pattern.

You will also notice that I used the same COB LED lights from the mgn Cube project, and they slide smoothly inside the extrusion profile. It's worth mentioning that the extrusion channels also support T-nuts, so you can attach any camera mount, filament holder, filters, lights and more.

This prototype enclosure was made especially for the Prusa MINI+, so its size is 48x48x48 cm and it holds the Prusa MINI+ and its original spool holder. The bottom has no panel, and a silicone sealing strip is installed to protect the table and the aluminum extrusions from damage. Also, when your 3D printer has a serious malfunction, it's easier to remove the enclosure without a bottom panel, which gives you more room to deal with the problem. Please note that I plan to design this enclosure not only for the Prusa MINI+ but also for a large selection of popular printers like the Ender 3 series, CR-10, Prusa MK3S+, Artillery and more.

There are a few more things I need to complete, such as testing the door mechanism, sealing the panels and developing a fume extraction/filtration system. Although I have a lot of work ahead, I'm glad that at least the hard part is over. I will no doubt need help with the next steps, and I will probably open a beta testers group in the new forum I am setting up on the BLVprojects.com site.

Feel free to check out the new BLV Discord server.

Sincerely,

Ben Levi

docs.title: Trademarks and the 3D community
docs.text:
We are all part of an amazing community.

A community of makers, a community of developers, a community of people who come willing to learn, experience together, and most importantly share. Out of this 3D community came many businesses and developers from all over the world. Some of them have not forgotten where they came from and what they represent.

Josef Průša is only one example of many. I admire him not because he sells 3D printers, but because he represents the idea of sharing that has driven the 3D community all along. He doesn't seem to be bothered by the dozens of clones sold on AliExpress and in Europe, and he still shares almost everything with the community he came from. I guess he knows that he is not just selling a printer, but a complete 3D printer package with support.

E3D is another good example, and so are many other projects that came out of the community. They are all willing to share CAD files, ideas, code and everything else the community needs.

I added a few random images so you don't get bored.

I think there are three main components here: a cohesive community, developers, and affordable 3D printer parts. Together they created a good infrastructure for the community to grow, and each one is just as important as the others. The improvised parts that were once part of our first printers were replaced by shiny, much more efficient parts. Parts that can be trusted and are available and affordable to everyone. Or are they? Are they truly affordable?

Well, I hope that a developer who patents something will understand that it's not fair to set a ridiculously high price for it. After all, for most of us it's just a hobby. Make no mistake, I don't justify patent infringement, but I'm very frustrated to see a component whose development, production and marketing cost less than $17 being sold for a few hundred dollars.

Naturally, community members searched for alternatives and found them in the Chinese market, which hurried to grab the opportunity and offer similar products at a lower, more reasonable price. Very quickly, IPP/IPR claims began to get AliExpress stores banned from time to time, and it still happens today. I recently tested a couple of nice Chinese CHT clones. Even so, I then bothered to buy 4 pcs of the original Bondtech CHT nozzle. Why? Because Bondtech introduced a real innovation, had to pay patent licenses, and still offers it at a fair price. That is much less than others who offer zero innovation, throw names of exotic metals into the air and demand a fortune. Well done, Bondtech!

The Bondtech CHT nozzles I bought for my own use - amazing results.

Related to that, I woke up one morning and, to my surprise, found out that my project had been stolen. At least that's what I understood from the messages some of my friends sent me. It turned out that FYSETC had registered a trademark on my project without asking me first. They were not the only ones, and it's not just my project but many others too. After a few video calls and chats with close Chinese friends, the situation became clearer. A cold war had been going on beneath the surface for a long time. IPR/IPP claims had gotten a few stores banned for weeks and months, which raised concerns among Chinese stores and manufacturers. Gradually they began to register trademarks. Most of them wanted to make sure they wouldn't be banned if someone filed an IPP/IPR complaint. Soon enough, others were doing it too, maybe just out of panic. What is happening there now is complete chaos.

A Chinese trademark registration I didn't even know about.

You're probably asking what I did about it.

In the past, a decent CoreXY 3D printer would have cost over $2,800. The BLV project started as an idea for an accurate and reliable printer that is also affordable, with a BOM price of around $1,000. Inspired by the 3D community, I promised myself that if it turned out good enough, I would share everything with the community. I never expected it to become so popular. A large part of that is thanks to the knowledge I gained from the community and to the AliExpress stores that offered parts at an affordable price. You may be wondering why I keep saying "affordable" at every opportunity. So let me tell you something about myself.

I was born into a good family. When I was young, my father got cancer and later passed away, and very quickly we became poor. A computer, a game console and sometimes even food became a dream I could only enjoy when I visited friends. I worked hard every day after school to help my family, graduated high school successfully, saved money and went to university. That's why the concept of affordability has a special meaning for me. Now you can guess what my response was to the trademark issue with FYSETC.

After many conversations, I told them how disappointed I was that they didn't share this decision with me. In the end, we came to a kind of understanding. I asked them not to prevent competition. As long as they don't ban anyone else without my permission and keep things affordable and fairly priced, I don't have a problem with it, at least for now. For the record, the only time I had to file an IPP/IPR complaint was against a factory that cloned the metal kit incorrectly, which led to dozens of complaints even though I didn't design their parts.

The next BLV hotend setup? Testing it soon.

I tried to map the manufacturers that provide parts for the BLV project:

  • FYSETC: currently the FYSETC store is a supplier of the BLV Cube kit, and I wrote an honest review of it. They manufacture many parts suitable for the BLV project, and they started selling the Spider V2.2 board, which I now use with a 48V system (absolutely crazy fast) and I am very happy with it. They also sell the BLV Ender 3 Pro metal kit (the files are free for everyone). Disclosure: they gave me a symbolic discount on the first kit, and that's it.
  • Blurolls: Peter was the first to support the BLV project and truly believed in it. He made the first kit and is still a supplier of the BLV Cube kit and the Lite kit, which costs under $500. He also provides many high-quality parts for the BLV project. Blurolls is the only manufacturer of the BLV metal kit, providing more than 65 CNC-machined aluminum parts at an unbelievable price of $110. Although the BLV project is open source, the BLV metal kit that came later is not fully open source. Only the X-carriage CAD files were published. We have an agreement: I gave him my work for free, and in return he sells the parts at the lowest price he can afford. No one else could promise me a lower price than his, and many tried. Please note that the FYSETC kits contain the official Blurolls BLV metal kit.
  • Mellow: you all know the Mellow store, and "high quality" is its middle name. Mellow will produce the new carbon X-axis for the BLV Cube, and I will include a few of their next products in the next update. I also made a whole new setup for the Mellow NF-Sunrise hotend/extruder. Their idlers and pulleys are the highest-quality yet affordable ones I have found for the BLV project. A well-known quality manufacturer that I respect.
  • LDO: they started supporting a few community projects, and the Orbiter and BLV are just two examples. LDO offers an excellent set of stepper motors for the BLV project. I tested their new LDO-42STH48-2504AC 2.5A steppers with FYSETC HV5160 drivers, with insane results over 300 hours of testing. Highly recommended. I am going to test the new Orbiter V2.0 by LDO with the Rapido hotend. Many thanks to my friend Róbert Lőrincz for the effort he has put into the amazing Orbiter V2.0 extruder project.
  • Trianglelab: a well-known manufacturer producing high-quality parts for many projects. I adapted the Dragon hotend and the Matrix extruder/hotend as soon as they came out. I am going to test the new Rapido hotend with Róbert Lőrincz's new Orbiter V2.0 extruder.
  • Funssor: provides frames and more for the BLV project at very affordable prices.
  • Haldis: I am testing new hotend setups for high-speed printing, but there are no approved parts yet.
  • CNA Mechanical Parts Store: offers a variety of linear rails and other affordable mechanical parts that I bought and tested myself. I lost a lot of money on cheap linear rails until I bought rails from CNA. Excellent linear rails at a reasonable price.
  • BOM links: all the products and stores that are part of the BOM. I tested and approved most of them myself, and some were suggested by community members.

Please feel free to provide parts for the BLV project, including printed parts, as long as you don't take advantage of or manipulate the project's license terms. Please respect the 3D community and don't ban competition.

And a small piece of advice for our Chinese friends, who have become an integral part of the 3D community. My dear friends, please try to be as transparent as possible and share with us the decisions related to developers and projects. Please communicate with us, and don't hesitate to ask and share your thoughts.

And for our great community: I see each member who has started a shared project as a partner. For those of you who decide to start a company or just sell products, I'm begging you, please do not forget where you came from. You are part of the 3D community, so please don't see us only as something to be exploited for money.

Please, don't take us back to a time when a 3D printer was just a dream.

Sincerely,

Ben Levi - BLV project developer
